A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DPCore research. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables and figures are readable and support comparison despite substantial restructuring.

before.justification: v2 reports original DPCore classification and segmentation experiments, component ablations, sensitivity analyses and repeated-domain adaptation results.

after.justification: v3 reports original DPCore benchmark results, prompt-transfer experiments, robustness analyses and alternative-reference-data evaluations.

M1.justification: The core prompt alignment, coreset and weighted-update procedure remain. v3 adds an entropy-filtered public-reference procedure for unavailable source data (Appendix F.2). DPCore-B retains v2's DPCore-DU buffering procedure despite renaming. v3 describes sigma as standard deviation rather than variance, without establishing whether the implementation changed.

E1.justification: The four principal classification and segmentation benchmarks remain. v3 adds STL10 images as replacement reference data and evaluates PTTA streams with local class correlation (Appendices E.3 and F.2), providing limited additional data and scenario coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds RoTTA, Yang et al.'s BDG (labeled BGD in Table 1), and C-MAE to ImageNet-C CSC comparisons, and C-MAE to segmentation comparisons. Its batch-size analysis adds Tent, CoTTA and ViDA comparators. SAR is omitted from the computational comparison, while segmentation methods omitted from the main summary remain in the appendix.

E3.justification: The main CDC protocol changes from uniform domain/duration sampling to Dirichlet sampling with delta=1; the earlier protocol remains as CDC-2D. Reported main settings change from learning rate 0.1 to 0.01, four to eight prompt tokens, and the entire source dataset to 300 examples. v3 also specifies batch size 64 across methods, whereas v2 explicitly compares against ViDA at 50.

E4.justification: v3 adds cross-domain prompt-transfer controls, ten random domain orders, Dirichlet-frequency sensitivity and a normalization-layer ablation, and substantially expands batch-size and source-data analyses (Figures 3–6, Table 3 and Appendix D.1). v2's ten-round continual-adaptation experiment is absent; the new ten-order experiment addresses a different robustness question.

E5.justification: v3 Table 9 newly reports a standard deviation of 0.7 for the ten random CDC-2D distribution results retained from v2 Table 15. This adds dispersion reporting without establishing additional runs.

E6.justification: Under revised reported settings, DPCore's CSC error changes from 40.5% to 39.9% on ImageNet-C and 18.4% to 15.4% on CIFAR10-C; CSC segmentation mIoU changes from 62.8 to 62.5. Matched CDC/CDC-2D tables retain DPCore's 43.2% but revise ViDA from 50.3% to 51.8%. New Dirichlet, PTTA and transfer results further expand the evidence; these are not all comparable-setting performance changes.

T1.justification: v3 Appendix C.4 restricts the simplified analysis to batch means and expresses the cluster center as an average of batch means, replacing v2's batch-statistics formulation and average-of-batches expression. The well-separatedness assumption, three propositions and basic proof arguments remain; no general robustness proof is added.

C1.justification: The central CDC proposal, DPCore contribution and overall superiority claims remain. v3 newly emphasizes requiring only 300 source examples and claims a 64% computation-time reduction in the abstract. That time claim is stronger than the evidence: Table 4's relative times of 1.8 versus ViDA's 2.8 imply approximately 35.7% reduction.

C2.justification: v3 substantially develops the convergence and negative-transfer explanation, linking prompt transfer to feature-space similarity (Section 3.3 and Appendix D.1). It expands applicability discussion to replacement reference data and explicitly argues that buffering becomes ineffective under frequent CDC transitions because accumulated batches mix domains (Appendix F.1), sharpening v2's general single-domain-batch limitation.

D1.justification: v3 adds a DPCore code-availability link and extensive implementation documentation: Gaussian prompt initialization, alpha=0.999, 50-step new-prompt optimization, validation-corruption selection, reference-data filtering and averaged propagation-cost calculations (Appendices B, C.3 and F). However, v2's explicit description of backbone fine-tuning on clean CIFAR10/100 is no longer stated.

R1.justification: The positioning against structured CTTA and methods requiring source-data warm-up remains. v3 adds references including C-MAE, BDG, continual prompt learning and representation transferability, explicitly classifies its adaptation as source-free, and expands comparisons with PTTA (Appendices A and E.3). These extend the existing research context without redefining the central contribution.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method and discussion are extensively rewritten. v3 introduces separate preliminaries and CDC-formulation sections, moves related work and formal propositions into the appendix, and reorganizes supplementary material into Sections A–G. The title, author list and component terminology also change.

P2.justification: v3 substantially redraws and expands the method overview, combines coreset growth with new analysis panels, and adds CDC timeline and sensitivity plots. Segmentation summaries are consolidated, detailed tables move to the appendix, and batch-size results become comparative plots. These are substantial changes to visual organization beyond numerical updates or pagination.

improvement.justification: v3 makes the method easier to reproduce and assess through implementation details, transfer controls, broader comparisons and clearer failure conditions. The net improvement is limited by removal of v2's ten-round adaptation evidence and new reporting errors: the abstract's 64% time reduction is unsupported by Table 4, and Table 2 reports C-MAE's CDC mean as 58.7 although its listed round scores average 59.5.
